plan.contextChunk: This figure shows a uniform thin disk twice, in two side-by-side views. The left view looks straight down the rotation axis: a blue-shaded circle with x pointing up, y pointing right, and z labeled at the center where the axis emerges from the page. A double-headed arrow from center to outer edge is labeled R, a second arrow labeled r reaches a thin orange ring concentric with the rim, and a short arrow labeled dr points at that ring's width. The right view redraws the disk in oblique perspective as a shaded ellipse with an orange rim, z vertical, y to the right, x coming toward the lower left; a curved arrow loops around z to show the sense of rotation, and an arrow labeled r runs from the center to an element on the ring labeled dm. Showing the ring face-on and in perspective ties the annular strip of width dr to the mass element dm at one distance from the axis. The pairing motivates finding the moment of inertia by summing thin rings, each carrying all its mass at radius r.

interactions.label: Ring radius r / R
interactions.teaches: Mass at larger radius contributes disproportionately more to the disk's moment of inertia because each ring's contribution is weighted by r²

demo_steps.title: Identify the ring element
demo_steps.narration: The orange strip is not a small patch: it is a full annular ring at radius r from the z-axis. This ring is the mass element dm used in the moment-of-inertia integral.

demo_steps.title: Move the same mass farther out
demo_steps.narration: Drag the radius outward and watch the same type of ring move toward the rim. The contribution indicator grows rapidly because the integrand contains r² dm, not just dm.

demo_steps.title: Change the amount of mass in the ring
demo_steps.narration: Widening dr makes the annular strip cover more area, so dm increases. The ring still represents material all at approximately the same radius r when dr is small.

demo_steps.title: Connect the two views
demo_steps.narration: Switch to the perspective view: the orange ellipse is the same ring, now seen as a tilted disk rotating about the z-axis. The dm label marks one piece of that full circular ring.

interactionPlan.keyInsight: A disk can be built from thin rings, and rings near the rim matter much more for rotational inertia because every bit of their mass is multiplied by r².
interactionPlan.reconstructionNotes: Use a two-view layout inspired by the source: a face-on circular disk on the left and an oblique elliptical disk on the right. Blue translucent shading should fill the disk, with the active annulus highlighted in orange in both views. The ring radius slider should move the annulus concentrically outward or inward in the circular view and to the matching elliptical radius in the perspective view; keep the annulus inside the disk by clamping its outer edge at R. The dr slider should visibly thicken or thin the orange strip and scale the dm/contribution indicator. In face-on emphasis, make the left disk brighter and the right disk slightly dimmed; in perspective emphasis, reverse that emphasis. Include the labels R, r, dr, dm, axes x/y/z, a curved rotation arrow about z, and a compact formula callout dI = r² dm near the growing contribution indicator.

authoredContext:
Integrating to find the moment of inertia of a two-dimensional object is a little bit trickier, but one shape is commonly done at this level of study—a uniform thin disk about an axis through its center (the figure).

Calculating the moment of inertia for a thin disk about an axis through its center.

Figure shows a uniform thin disk of radius r that rotates about a Z axis that passes through its center.

Since the disk is thin, we can take the mass as distributed entirely in the xy-plane. We again start with the relationship for the surface mass density, which is the mass per unit surface area. Since it is uniform, the surface mass density σ is constant:
